Delaporte Distribution

Source: R/delaporte.R
Delaporte.Rd

Density, distribution function, quantile function, and random generation for the Delaporte distribution in a mean parameterization.

Usage

ddelaporte(x, mu, rho, k, log = FALSE)

pdelaporte(q, mu, rho, k, lower.tail = TRUE, log.p = FALSE)

qdelaporte(p, mu, rho, k, lower.tail = TRUE, log.p = FALSE)

rdelaporte(n, mu, rho, k)

Arguments

x

vector of (non-negative integer) quantiles.

mu

vector of means \(\mu \geq 0\).

rho

vector of shares \(0 \leq \rho \leq 1\) of the mean that come from the negative binomial (gamma-mixed) component.

k

vector of (positive) negative binomial size (shape) parameters.

log, log.p

logical; if TRUE, probabilities p are given as log(p).

q

vector of quantiles.

lower.tail

logical; if TRUE (default), probabilities are \(P(Y \leq y)\), otherwise \(P(Y > y)\).

p

vector of probabilities.

n

number of observations. If length(n) > 1, the length is taken to be the number required.

Value

ddelaporte gives the probability mass, pdelaporte the distribution function, qdelaporte the quantile function, and rdelaporte random deviates. The length of the result is determined by n for rdelaporte, and is the maximum of the lengths of the numerical arguments for the other functions.

Details

A Delaporte random variable is the sum of two independent counts, $$Y = A + B, \quad A \sim \mathrm{Poisson}((1 - \rho)\mu), \quad B \sim \mathrm{NB}(\mathrm{size} = k, \mathrm{mean} = \rho\mu),$$ so that $$E[Y] = \mu, \qquad \mathrm{Var}[Y] = \mu + \frac{(\rho\mu)^2}{k}.$$ Equivalently it is a Poisson distribution whose rate is a shifted gamma variable. \(\rho = 0\) gives the Poisson distribution with mean \(\mu\) and \(\rho = 1\) the negative binomial distribution with mean \(\mu\) and size \(k\) (NB2 with \(\alpha = 1/k\)). Both endpoints are accepted here.

In the \((\alpha, \beta, \lambda)\) parameterization of the Delaporte package, \(\alpha = k\), \(\beta = \rho\mu / k\) and \(\lambda = (1 - \rho)\mu\).

Probabilities are computed by summing the convolution of the two components on the log scale (all terms are positive). Both tails are computed directly from the same decomposition, so lower.tail = FALSE is accurate far into the upper tail. Random deviates are generated as the sum of independent Poisson and negative binomial draws. The work per probability grows linearly with the count.

References

Ruohonen, M. (1988). On a model for the claim number process. ASTIN Bulletin, 18(1), 57-68.

Vose, D. (2008). Risk Analysis: A Quantitative Guide (3rd ed.). Wiley.

Examples

ddelaporte(0:6, mu = 2, rho = 0.5, k = 1.5)
#> [1] 0.17097491 0.27355986 0.23936488 0.15501726 0.08457559 0.04172700 0.01939783
# rho = 0 is Poisson, rho = 1 is negative binomial
all.equal(ddelaporte(0:10, mu = 2, rho = 0, k = 1.5), dpois(0:10, 2))
#> [1] TRUE
all.equal(ddelaporte(0:10, mu = 2, rho = 1, k = 1.5),
          dnbinom(0:10, size = 1.5, mu = 2))
#> [1] TRUE
pdelaporte(5, mu = 2, rho = 0.5, k = 1.5)
#> [1] 0.9652195
qdelaporte(c(0.5, 0.95), mu = 2, rho = 0.5, k = 1.5)
#> [1] 2 5
set.seed(3)
y <- rdelaporte(5000, mu = 4, rho = 0.6, k = 2)
c(mean = mean(y), var = var(y))   # theory: 4 and 4 + 2.4^2 / 2 = 6.88
#>     mean      var 
#> 4.011400 6.978266
